content:
Apple has responded to Epic's opposition to its request to halt lower court proceedings related to App Store commissions, with the Supreme Court currently reviewing parts of the case. Here is a breakdown of what it means.

Apple says Epic's arguments are wrong

Last month, the Supreme Court agreed to review whether Apple was correctly held in contempt for collecting commissions on purchases made through the App Store outside the United States.

The dispute stems from a 2021 injunction requiring Apple to let developers direct users to purchasing options outside the App Store. While the injunction did not explicitly prohibit charging commissions on such transactions, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers later ruled that Apple's implementation violated the order and held the company in contempt. Apple has been challenging that ruling.

As soon as the Supreme Court agreed to review the ruling, Apple asked to pause lower court proceedings to determine what kind of commission, if any, it could charge on such purchases.

Apple argues that the Supreme Court's decision could eliminate the need for those proceedings altogether or fundamentally change their direction, so it wants the lower court to wait and see rather than push forward with work that may later need to be revisited.

Epic sees things differently. As we reported yesterday, the company argues that asking to halt the lower court proceedings while the Supreme Court reviews the contempt ruling is "Apple's third attempt to delay the inevitable: a hearing to assess the fees Apple is charging on steered transactions."

In its filing opposing Apple's request, the Fortnite developer also said: "Even if the Supreme Court agrees with Apple on the contempt argument, the lower court will still need to conduct further proceedings, particularly on the question of commissions, and those proceedings will likely be nearly identical regardless of whether the Supreme Court reviews the contempt ruling."

Now, Apple has responded to Epic's opposition, once again arguing that Epic's arguments are based on faulty assumptions, misrepresent the scope of the Supreme Court's review, and underestimate its impact on the lower court proceedings:

And

And

"Epic's primary argument is that the Supreme Court's resolution of the contempt issue will have no impact on this Court's proceedings (Opp. 6-10). Epic therefore urges this Court to proceed immediately with the 'remand proceedings' (Opp. 4). Epic is wrong. The only basis for any 'remand proceedings' is this Court's civil contempt finding. (...)"

And

Ultimately, Apple's response to Epic's opposition is to restate its original position while methodically refuting each of Epic's reasons for why the lower court should deny Apple's request to stay the case while the Supreme Court reviews the contempt ruling.

Apple also points out twice that, in its view, the Supreme Court will be deciding "whether the Ninth Circuit applied the wrong legal standard," and Apple says this could invalidate the contempt finding or require the appeals court to reconsider it under the correct standard.

Finally, Apple asks that, if Judge Gonzalez Rogers denies its request to stay, she pause the proceedings anyway so the company can petition the Ninth Circuit or the Supreme Court to continue holding things up while the Supreme Court reviews the contempt ruling.
